title: Large TESS flares on CPV host M dwarfs are followed by lasting dip-pattern changes in about 9% of cases; the dips rearrange without net collapse, and flares cause few of all changes
abstract: Complex periodic variables (CPVs) are young M dwarfs with sharp dips at the rotation period, probably from magnetically held material near corotation. An earlier report suggested that flares sometimes make the dips collapse, but no sample test existed. We used all TESS 2-minute sectors (2018-2026) of 114 CPV hosts and of 200 non-host rapid rotators of the same period, colour and age range, and detected 5,493 flares. For each flare, we compared the folded rotational pattern before and after the flare and ranked the change against random times in the same light curve. For flares above 1e33 erg, with the after-window delayed by 0.5 d to remove flare light, the mean rank on hosts is 0.574 (95% interval 0.550-0.603; 537 flares, 87 stars; no effect = 0.5). About 9% (6-13%) of these flares are followed by a large change in excess of chance. Controls give 0.477 (0.441-0.514); the difference is 0.097 (0.051-0.141). Flares of 1e32-1e33 erg give no effect (0.493). The change is within about 0.5 d of the flare. The dips weakened after 10.3% and grew after 8.4% of host flares; injections show that at most 10% of large flares remove half of the dips (95% bound). Large flares occur at only 3.2% of the times of the largest pattern changes (1.45% at all times), and flares do not prefer dip phases. Thus large flares disturb the corotating material, which shows magnetic coupling, but they do not remove or supply a net amount of it and cause few of all pattern changes. Limitations: the test shows association, not proven cause; time resolution is about 0.5 d; energies are approximate; one band; the 0.5 d delay was chosen after a flare-light effect was seen in controls. Code, derived tables, figures and hashes are included; TESS files are not.

display.caption: Mean rank of the before/after pattern change D for flares of E >= 1e33 erg, ranked in the random-time null of the same light curve (0.5 = no effect; bands are 95% star-bootstrap intervals). A: split time moved away from the flare (1-day windows). B and C: the after-window delayed by up to 0.5 d (1-day and 1-rotation windows). The host effect stays when the after-window is delayed; the control effect (remaining flare light) goes away.

A: mean rank of D by flare energy with the after-window delayed 0.5 d. Host flares above 1e33 erg are followed by pattern changes; smaller flares and control flares are not. B: fractions of host flares (CPV sectors, E >= 1e33 erg) after which the sharp dip amplitude fell or rose (rank < 0.05 or > 0.95), observed and after injected dip losses or gains. Falls and rises occur at similar rates, so there is no net collapse.

Five host flares with the largest pattern changes when the after-window is delayed by 0.5 d (blue: before-window, orange: after-window; right: folded profiles), and one long-decay flare drawn with the standard after-window, which contains the flare decay.

Bouma et al. 2024 reported that flares seem to induce sudden dip collapses once every few months. We confirm a flare-related change at that rate, but the changes are rearrangements in both directions, not net collapses.
